context: A lecture on spider silk and attempts to copy it

cues.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about spider silk and the attempts to produce it artificially. First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about a material that engineers have envied for more than a century: spider silk. Weight for weight, the toughest kinds of spider silk can absorb more energy before they break than almost any fibre we know how to make, including those used in protective vests for the police.

Let's begin with how a spider actually makes it. Inside the spider, silk isn't a thread at all. It's kept in glands in the abdomen as a liquid, a very concentrated solution of protein. People often assume that it hardens when it meets the air, rather like glue drying. But that isn't what happens. The silk only becomes solid as it is pulled out of the body. As the spider draws it through narrow tubes called spinnerets, the protein molecules line up and lock together.

A single spider may produce as many as seven kinds of silk, each from a different gland. Take the familiar round web you see in the garden. The frame and the spokes are made of what's called dragline silk, which is the strongest type. But the spiral that actually catches the insects is quite different. It's extremely elastic, so that it stretches rather than snaps when a fly hits it, and it's covered in tiny drops of glue.

Silk isn't only used for webs. Spiders wrap their eggs in it, and young spiders use it to travel. A spiderling climbs to a high point, lets out a thread, and is lifted by the breeze. They can travel enormous distances in this way. Sailors have reported spiders landing on ships hundreds of kilometres from land.

Humans have been making use of spider silk for a very long time. It was never woven into cloth on any scale, but the ancient Greeks placed spider webs on wounds to stop them bleeding. And until the middle of the twentieth century, the fine cross-hairs that you look through in telescopes were made of spider silk, because it was thinner and more even than any wire.

So why don't we simply farm spiders, as we have farmed silkworms for thousands of years? People have tried. The most famous attempt was in Madagascar, where over a million spiders were collected to make a single golden cape. But it took several years, and it's not a practical industry. The basic problem is that spiders are cannibals. If you keep them close together, they eat one another.

Scientists have therefore tried to get other organisms to make the protein instead. The genes for spider silk have been put into bacteria, into yeast, and, most famously, into goats, which then produced the silk protein in their milk. Making the protein, though, turns out to be the easy part. The real difficulty lies in copying the spinning process, and so far artificial fibres have been weaker than the natural ones.

Even so, there is great interest in the material. Clothing companies have experimented with it, but the most promising work is in medicine. Silk is not rejected by the body, and it breaks down slowly. Researchers have used silk tubes to help damaged nerves grow back together, and early results have been encouraging.
Next time, we'll look at another natural material that engineers would like to copy, which is the shell of the sea snail.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
